extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of English literature and literary criticism (undergraduate/graduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Explaining and evaluating archetypal criticism (principles, methods, classifications) with emphasis on Northrop Frye's synthesis of Jungian myth theory and literary analysis. Useful for learning how to apply archetypal frameworks to literary texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of archetype
rubrics_metrics.description: “archetype, borrowed from Jung, means a primordial image, a part of the collective unconscious, the psychic residue of numberless experiences of the same kind, and thus part of the inherited response pattern of the race.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archetypes are described as primordial images, symbols, characters and motifs that stir a primary feeling across cultures; they belong to the collective unconscious rather than individual experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for approving an archetype
rubrics_metrics.description: “An image, symbol or motif should recur throughout literary history for it to be approved as an archetype.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recurrence across historical periods and cultures is the decisive test for designating an element as an archetype.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jungian individual-psychic archetypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Jung delineates four archetypes of man: Persona, Self, Shadow and Anima/Animus — Persona (the mask we present), Self (unified unconsciousness and consciousness), Shadow (repressed instincts, desires, shortcomings), Anima/Animus (feminine image in male psyche/male image in female psyche).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to map individual characters' psychic structures; Jung locates archetypes as patterns of psychic energy that often manifest in dreams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twelve universal mythical character archetypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Jung (as presented) identifies twelve character archetypes: Ruler, Creator, Sage, Innocent, Explorer, Rebel, Hero, Wizard, Jester, Everyman, Lover and Caregiver; these are further categorized into ego types, soul types and self-types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These labels are tools for comparative description; critics can group characters into these types to show recurring mythic roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archetypal situations, subjects and images (catalogue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Archetypal situations include rivalry between brothers, longing for a father figure, country bumpkin coming to city, intergenerational tension; subjects include birth, love, war, guilt, redemption, death; images include lion, eagle, ox, serpent, dove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a text, look for these recurrent situations/subjects/images as signs of archetypal patterning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful vs meaningless criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Meaningful criticism contributes to a systematic structure of knowledge about a work; meaningless criticism is rhetorical verbosity, pseudo-propositions and abstract value-statements that do not help systematic understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should avoid over-glorified verbosity and unsupported value-judgments; aim for analyses that build coherent, testable frameworks rather than mere rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value-free scientific approach to criticism (Frye)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye stressed a ‘value-free science of criticism’ and dismissed value-judgments as largely sociological and psychological reflections rather than objective knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a systematic, law-seeking method (inductive + deductive) rather than evaluative moralizing; focus on structural and mythic patterns rather than taste-based verdicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centripetal (structural) vs centrifugal (historical) criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Centripetal criticism moves inward toward the structure of the text (Formalist), centrifugal criticism moves outward from the text to the outer world (historical/contextual).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the strengths and limits of both approaches; Frye recommends synthesizing them in archetypal criticism (see next criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Archetypal criticism as synthesis of structural and historical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Archetypal criticism synthesizes structural (centripetal) and historical (centrifugal) criticism by interpreting texts with respect to cultural patterns (myth, ritual, race, nation or social group) while attending to structural imagery and motifs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply both close textual analysis (structure, imagery) and historical/cultural tracing (origins of motifs and genres) to reveal archetypal networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive and deductive methods in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye advocates a combination of inductive and deductive analysis: inductive (study works to discover patterns) and deductive (apply general truths/myths to explicate particulars).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inductive work-history comparison to build hypotheses about mythic patterns, then test and apply them deductively to particular texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic's staged interventions (multidisciplinary interpretive roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye proposes ordered interventions: editor (clean text), rhetorician (examine form), philologist (word choice/significance), literary social historian (evolution of myth/ritual), literary psychologist (psychological/psychoanalytic readings), literary historian/anthropologist (trace archetype sources).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation should be collaborative/multifaceted: consult different specialist methods at different stages to reconstruct archetypal meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four phases of myth (Frye's classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye formulates four phases of myth: (1) dawn/spring/birth — myths of birth, revival, resurrection (comedic sense); (2) zenith/summer/marriage/triumph — apotheosis and romance; (3) sunset/autumn/death — myths of fall, violent death (degeneration); (4) darkness/winter/dissolution — triumph of dark powers, collapse, satire/irony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map a narrative's dominant phase to these seasonal/mythic stages to determine its mythoi and subordinate character types (father/mother; companion/bride; traitor/siren; ogre/witch).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping seasons to genres (mythoi)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seasons are associated with genres: Summer – comedy; Spring – romance; Autumn – satire; Winter – tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the season→genre mapping as a heuristic when classifying a work's dominant mythic orientation, remembering Frye's use of seasonal analogies for tonal/structural features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quest myth as origin of genres
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye regards the Quest Myth as the original starting point of all genres: the critic moves from general myth to particular text (inductive) and studies sacred religious scriptures as primary documents for archetypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking genre origins, trace quasireligious or ritual quest narratives and show how their motifs generate later genre conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-sphere schema for archetypal images
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye outlines five spheres: human, animal, vegetation, mineral and water — each having comic vs tragic correspondences (e.g., human: symposium/communion/order vs tyranny/anarchy; animal: flock/doves vs beasts/dragons; vegetable: garden/rose vs sinister forest; mineral: city/temple vs ruins/cross; water: fourfold river vs sea/flood/leviathan).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse imagery in a text by locating it within these spheres and contrasting its comic vs tragic manifestations to read its archetypal vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of archetypal criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Archetypal criticism studies an individual work as part of the whole web of literature, liberates criticism from determinism of social history, and makes criticism more scientific by giving laws that govern literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use archetypal frameworks to situate works historically and comparatively, demonstrating patterning across texts rather than only isolated readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disadvantages / limits of archetypal criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Main disadvantages: reductionism (reducing literature to a mono-myth/quest myth), arbitrariness in taxonomy/categorisation, excessive emphasis on uniformity that dismisses uniqueness, crude/unverifiable 'myth hunting', and redundancy in postmodern literature where genre boundaries blur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of overgeneralization: explicitly justify taxonomic decisions, attend to uniqueness of texts, and recognize when experimental/postmodern works resist archetypal classification (example: Waiting for Godot as tragicomedy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of recurrence and cultural universality for archetypal claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Archetypal critics argue universality by pointing to recurring patterns embedded in the cultural psyche; the archetypal hypothesis requires images/patterns to be shared across cultures and history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support archetypal claims with cross-cultural and diachronic evidence rather than isolated parallels; distinguish genuine universals from coincidental resemblance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frye's stance on religious/mythic sources and the critic's focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye treats sacred religious scriptures as primary documents to study archetypes and argues criticism concerns itself with the conceivable (mythic/imagistic meaning) rather than the explainable (origins).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tracing archetypes, foreground canonical mythic/religious texts and their narrative patterns as source material for later literary uses, but avoid making unverifiable claims about psychological origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frye's rejection of deconstruction and subjectivist approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye vehemently dismissed deconstruction as 'suicidal and destructive' and rejected Derrida's metaphors of centre and origin that allow 'free play'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a systematic, center-seeking framework rather than a purely deconstructive, relativizing posture when using Frye's archetypal method; be aware this stance is contested by later theory.
